text: Ammonites were sea animals that lived inside coiled shells. They were [[cephalopod|cephalopods]], the group that includes squid, octopuses and cuttlefish. A squid-like body with [[tentacle|tentacles]] poked out of the open end of the shell.

They appeared about 400 million years ago, survived the [[@great-dying|Great Dying]] by a whisker, and became common in the seas of the dinosaur age. Then, 66 million years ago, they died out in the same disaster that ended the giant dinosaurs. Their shells are among the most common [[fossil|fossils]] on Earth.

st.prompt: Ammonites are often used to work out the age of rocks. Why are they so good for this?

options.t: Each kind lived for a short time, so it marks a particular slice of history
Their shells contain a tiny clock

st.reveal: Ammonites changed quickly, so each species lasted only a short time, sometimes less than a million years. They also spread widely through the seas. Find a particular kind in a rock and you know roughly when that rock formed, even on the other side of the world.

sec.t:
Most ammonites were palm-sized or smaller. The largest known, found in Germany, had a shell about as wide as a grown man is tall. Some ammonites were not neatly coiled at all. Later kinds grew shells shaped like hooks, paper clips or loose corkscrews.

The name comes from Ammon, an Egyptian god often shown with curled ram's horns. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder called these fossils "horns of Ammon". In Alberta, Canada, some ammonite shells kept their shimmering mother-of-pearl layer for 70 million years. Polished, it becomes a rainbow-coloured gem called ammolite.

Their closest living relatives are squid and octopuses, not the nautilus, even though the nautilus has a similar chambered shell. An [[@octopus-smart|octopus]] and an ammonite shared an ancestor long ago. The octopus lineage lost its outer shell and the ammonites kept theirs.

In Nepal, the Kali Gandaki river carries black stones that break open to show ammonite fossils. Hindus call these stones shaligrams and worship them as a form of Lord Vishnu. Pilgrims travel to the river valley near Muktinath, and shaligrams are kept in homes and temples in India and [[@nepal|Nepal]]. The rocks formed in an ancient sea before the Himalayas rose.

In England, ammonites were once called snakestones. A legend in the town of Whitby said that a saint had turned snakes to stone. Fossil sellers sometimes carved snake heads onto them for tourists. [[@mary-anning|Mary Anning]] sold ammonites on the beach at Lyme Regis.

Because ammonites changed fast and spread widely, [[geologist|geologists]] use them to [[@fossil-age|date rocks]]. Each [[species|species]] lasted only a short time. A geologist who finds a particular kind knows roughly when that layer formed. In [[@gujarat-rann|Kutch]], in Gujarat, rocks packed with ammonites help geologists date the layers laid down when that area was a shallow sea in the Jurassic.

When [[@extinction|the asteroid]] struck 66 million years ago, the seas changed fast. Ammonite babies were tiny and drifted near the surface, where the [[foodchain|food chain]] collapsed. The nautilus, which lays larger eggs and lives in deeper water, came through. The ammonites, after more than 300 million years, did not.

text: Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. It becomes polluted when other things get mixed in: soot, dust, smoke, and gases such as nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide and ground-level [[ozone|ozone]]. Most of it comes from burning things. Car and truck engines, coal power plants, factories, cooking fires and burning crop stubble all send smoke into the sky.
The worst part is often invisible. Tiny particles called PM2.5 are so small they get deep into our lungs. We clean the air mostly by burning less, and by filtering the smoke from what we still burn.

st.prompt: PM2.5 is the tiny dust that does the most harm to our lungs. How does one speck compare with a human hair?
st.reveal: A hair is about 70 thousandths of a millimetre wide. A PM2.5 speck is under 2.5. That is small enough to slip past the nose and throat, deep into the lungs.

sec.t:
The same smoke can be harmless one day and choking the next. Weather decides. On windy days, pollution blows away and spreads thin. On cold, still winter nights, a layer of warm air can sit on top of cooler air near the ground, like a lid on a pot. Smoke gets trapped underneath.

That is part of why [[@delhi|Delhi]] has some of its dirtiest air in November and December. Vehicles, building dust, industry and the burning of leftover straw on farms in [[@punjab|Punjab]] and Haryana all add to it, and the still air keeps it close to the ground.

Nature makes some pollution too. Dust storms blow in from the [[@desert-life|Thar Desert]] before the [[monsoon|monsoon]]. [[@volcano|Volcanoes]] puff out ash and gas. In September 2020, smoke from [[@forest-fires|huge wildfires]] turned the daytime sky over San Francisco a deep orange, and streetlights stayed on at noon. But in most big cities, people's own burning is the main source, and that is the part we can change.

When you breathe in, air travels down to millions of tiny bags in your [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]], where oxygen passes into your blood. Fine particles can travel all the way there. Over years, dirty air makes asthma worse and harms the heart and lungs. Children breathe faster than adults and are closer to car exhausts, so they take in more.

The World Health Organization says almost everyone on Earth breathes air dirtier than its guidelines. On bad days, health officials advise staying indoors more and skipping hard exercise outside.

Cleaner air has a few proven recipes. Filters on power plant chimneys catch soot. Devices called catalytic converters, fitted to car exhausts, turn some poisonous gases into safer ones. Better fuels and [[@electric-cars|electric cars]] help, and so do buses and metros that move many people at once.

In the early 2000s, Delhi switched its buses and autorickshaws to a cleaner gas called CNG. Across India, millions of families have swapped smoky wood and dung stoves for gas cooking, which helps the air inside homes. Air pollution also has a big cousin: the same burning that makes smog adds the gases behind [[@climate-change|climate change]].

text: The usual answer is Tristan da Cunha, a volcanic island in the South Atlantic Ocean. Fewer than 300 people live there, in one village called Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. The nearest place with people is Saint Helena, about 2,430 km away, roughly the straight-line distance from Delhi to Kanyakumari. South Africa is about 2,800 km away.

There is no airport. Supply and fishing ships come from Cape Town a few times a year, and the trip takes around a week. If you are counting islands where nobody lives, the loneliest of all is Bouvet Island, a frozen speck far to the south.

sec.h: Life at the edge of the map
sec.t:
Tristan is a single round volcano rising out of the sea, with a peak called Queen Mary's Peak at about 2,060 m. The village sits on the only flat strip of land, on the north coast.

The islanders grow potatoes in patches outside the village, raise sheep and cattle, and catch crawfish, a kind of lobster that is the island's main [[export|export]]. Money from selling stamps and coins with Tristan's name also helps. There is a school, a small hospital, a shop, a pub and a church.

Many islanders share just a few family names, handed down from the families who settled there in the 1800s. Everyone knows everyone. It is part of the United Kingdom's overseas [[territory|territories]].

Bouvet Island, which belongs to Norway, lies in the South Atlantic about 1,700 km from the coast of Antarctica. Over nine-tenths of it is covered by a [[glacier|glacier]], and it has no harbour. It is often called the most remote island on Earth.

Only scientists and a few [[expedition|expeditions]] have set foot on it, often by helicopter. Seals and penguins are the main residents. In 1964, a mysterious abandoned lifeboat was found on the island, and nobody ever found out where it came from.

India has remote islands too. The [[@andaman|Andaman and Nicobar Islands]] lie about 1,200 km from the mainland, closer to Myanmar and Indonesia than to Chennai. Lakshadweep's coral islands sit far out in the Arabian Sea.

The Pacific is full of lonely islands. [[@easter-island|Easter Island]], famous for its giant stone heads, is over 2,000 km from the nearest inhabited island. Pitcairn Island, home to fewer than 50 people, has one of the smallest populations of any territory in the world.

In the South Pacific lies Point Nemo, the spot in the ocean farthest from any land, about 2,700 km from the nearest shore. Space agencies even steer old satellites to crash into the ocean nearby, because nobody lives there.

Here's the strange part. When the International Space Station passes overhead, its crew about 400 km up are often the nearest humans to Point Nemo. The loneliest people on Earth's map may be the ones living on the [[@space-station|space station]], not on any island at all.

text: Rock forms in layers, like a stack of chapatis. The bottom ones were made first, so they're the oldest.
Layers of volcanic ash contain special [[atom|atoms]] that work like a clock. Scientists can measure their age very precisely.
If a [[fossil|fossil]] is sandwiched between two dated ash layers, its age must be somewhere in between.

quiz.prompt: A fossil lies between two ash layers. The ash below it is 68 million years old, and the ash above is 66 million years old. How old is the fossil?
quiz.reveal: The fossil was buried after the lower ash fell and before the upper ash covered it. So its age must lie in between. Scientists call this bracketing.

At the end, "dig" down through the pile. The bottom sheet is the oldest, just as in rock. Now slip a sheet out from the middle and see if a friend can work out which day it came from.
myth: Scientists use carbon dating to find out how old dinosaur fossils are.

Carbon dating only works for things up to about 50,000 years old. After that, almost no carbon-14 is left. Dinosaur fossils are tens of millions of years old, so scientists date the volcanic rock around them using other atoms, like potassium and uranium.

sec.t:
The first clue is simply the order of the layers. Mud and sand settle on top of what was there before, so going down means going back in time. [[geologist|Geologists]] call this relative dating. It tells you which fossil is older, but not by how many years.

Fossils themselves help match layers from place to place. In the early 1800s, an English canal digger named William Smith noticed that each rock layer held its own set of fossils, always in the same order. Using this, he made the first geological map of a whole country, Britain, in 1815.

Some fossils make excellent markers because the animals spread widely and changed quickly. [[@ammonites|Ammonites]], coiled sea animals, are a favourite. Each kind lived for only a short time, so finding a particular ammonite tells a geologist roughly when that rock formed, whether it's in England, Spiti or Madagascar.

{{story:ammonites}}

To put real numbers on the layers, scientists need atom clocks. When a volcano erupts, its ash contains tiny crystals. As the crystals form, they trap certain unstable atoms, such as a type of potassium. Over time these slowly change into another [[element|element]], at a steady and known rate. Measuring how much has changed tells you when the crystal formed.

Fossils rarely contain these clock atoms themselves, so scientists look for ash layers above and below them. That gives a range, like knowing a letter arrived sometime between Monday's post and Wednesday's.

Different clocks suit different ages. Carbon-14, the famous one, runs out after about 50,000 years, so it is used for things like [[mammoth|mammoth]] bones, ancient seeds and charcoal from old campfires. For dinosaurs and older fossils, scientists use slow clocks such as potassium and uranium, which keep ticking for billions of years.

The layer that marks the end of the dinosaurs is one of the most carefully dated rocks on Earth. It is full of [[iridium|iridium]], a metal common in [[asteroid|asteroids]] but rare in [[@earth-layers-crust|Earth's crust]]. That [[@iridium-evidence|iridium layer]] is found all over the world.

In 2013, a team led by Paul Renne measured ash just above and below it in Montana, USA. They got about 66 million years, give or take only about 11,000 years. That is like measuring the length of a 66 km road and being off by just 11 metres.

India has its own natural clocks: the [[@deccan|Deccan]] lava flows. About 66 million years ago, huge eruptions in western and central India poured out layer upon layer of lava. Scientists have dated many of those layers using atom clocks.

[[@dino-eggs|Dinosaur eggs]] and bones found at places like Jabalpur and in Gujarat lie in rocks just below or between these lava flows. So the lava acts like a set of dated bookends. Those fossils tell the story of the last [[@dinos-in-india|dinosaurs that lived in India]], right up to the time [[@extinction|the asteroid]] struck.

text: ऑक्टोपस भाग निकलने के लिए स्याही छोड़ता है। जब कोई भूखी मछली, सील या ईल हमला करती है, तो ऑक्टोपस गाढ़ी स्याही का एक बादल छोड़ता है और पानी की धार के सहारे तेज़ी से दूर निकल जाता है। [[predator|शिकारी]] के सामने बस एक धुंधला बादल रह जाता है, और इस बीच ऑक्टोपस [[@octopus-colour|रंग बदलकर]] छिप जाता है।

स्याही कई तरह से काम आ सकती है। बड़ा बादल धुएँ के परदे जैसा काम करता है। एक छोटा, चिपचिपा गोला पानी में लगभग ऑक्टोपस के आकार में लटका रह सकता है, जिससे शिकारी धोखा खाकर गलत निशाने पर झपट पड़ता है। और स्याही के कुछ रसायन थोड़ी देर के लिए शिकारी की आँखों में जलन पैदा कर सकते हैं या उसकी सूँघने की ताक़त कमज़ोर कर सकते हैं। ऑक्टोपस और भी कई तरीकों से भाग निकलने में उस्ताद हैं, जैसा तुम [[@octopus-smart|ऑक्टोपस कितने होशियार हैं]] में पढ़ सकते हो।

sec.t:
ऑक्टोपस की स्याही ज़्यादातर [[melanin|मेलानिन]] नाम के गहरे रंजक और लसलसे [[mucus|बलगम]] का मिश्रण होती है। मेलानिन वही रंजक है जो तुम्हारे बालों, [[@skin|त्वचा]] और आँखों को रंग देता है। स्याही एक स्याही की थैली में बनती और जमा रहती है। यह छोटी-सी थैली ऑक्टोपस की आँतों के पास होती है। ज़रूरत पड़ने पर ऑक्टोपस स्याही को अपनी कीप में दबा देता है, जहाँ वह बाहर धकेले जा रहे पानी में मिल जाती है।

बलगम की मात्रा से तय होता है कि स्याही क्या करेगी। पतली स्याही फैलकर एक चौड़ा बादल बना देती है। ज़्यादा बलगम वाली स्याही एक गोले की तरह जुड़ी रहती है। मेलानिन रोशनी को बहुत अच्छे से सोखता है, इसलिए पतला बादल भी गहरा दिखता है। वैज्ञानिक इन गोलों को स्यूडोमॉर्फ़ कहते हैं, यानी "नकली आकार"।

हर सेफ़ेलोपॉड गाढ़ी स्याही इस्तेमाल नहीं करता। गहरे समुद्र में रहने वाले कई ऑक्टोपस, जैसे कान जैसे पंखों वाले डम्बो ऑक्टोपस, के पास स्याही की थैली होती ही नहीं। सतह से बहुत नीचे के अँधेरे में काला बादल किसी काम का नहीं।

गहरे समुद्र के कुछ जीवों के पास दूसरी तरकीब है। अँधेरे, ठंडे पानी में रहने वाला वैम्पायर स्क्विड काले बादल की जगह चिपचिपे, चमकते बलगम का बादल छोड़ सकता है। नीली चिंगारियाँ शिकारी को चौंका या उलझा सकती हैं, और इस बीच वैम्पायर स्क्विड खिसक लेता है। जीवों की बनाई रोशनी को [[@bioluminescence|बायोल्यूमिनेसेंस]] कहते हैं। इसके दूर के रिश्तेदारों में भीमकाय [[@giant-squid|विशाल स्क्विड]] भी है, जो स्याही छोड़ सकता है।

लोग बहुत समय से सेफ़ेलोपॉड की स्याही इस्तेमाल करते आए हैं। कटलफ़िश से बनी भूरी सीपिया स्याही यूरोप में सदियों तक लिखने और चित्र बनाने के काम आई। "सीपिया" कटलफ़िश के लिए यूनानी शब्द है, और आज यह [[@photography-art|पुरानी तस्वीरों]] वाले लाल-भूरे रंग का नाम भी है।

स्क्विड और कटलफ़िश की स्याही खाना पकाने में भी इस्तेमाल होती है, ख़ासकर इटली और स्पेन में। यह पास्ता और चावल को चमकदार काला बना देती है, और उनमें समुद्र जैसा नमकीन स्वाद आ जाता है, जैसे इटली की काली स्पेगेटी में ([[@noodles-pasta|नूडल्स और पास्ता]] देखो)। पर कुदरत में स्याही का बस एक ही काम है: एक नरम, बिना हड्डी वाले जानवर को इतनी देर ज़िंदा रखना कि वह फिर से छिप सके।

text: When you write with a [[@pencils|pencil]], tiny flakes of graphite stick to the fibres on top of the paper. They don't soak in. An eraser is made of a soft, slightly sticky material that grips graphite more strongly than paper does. Rub it over the mark, and the flakes cling to the eraser instead.

The rubbing also wears the eraser away. Little crumbs roll up, carrying the graphite with them, and fall off. That keeps a clean surface touching the paper. So the grey crumbs you brush off the page are the pencil line, wrapped up and removed.

st.reveal: A good eraser is designed to wear away. As it rubs, its surface rolls up with graphite stuck to it and breaks off as crumbs, so a fresh, clean surface keeps touching the paper.

sec.t:
For centuries, people who used graphite or chalk rubbed out mistakes with soft, fresh bread, squeezed into a ball. It picked up the dust well enough. Some drawing artists still use bread or a soft, putty-like eraser that works in the same way.

Others used wax, or rough stones like pumice to scrape marks off parchment. Scribes who wrote in ink on animal skin sometimes shaved off mistakes with a knife.

Early rubber had problems. It went sticky and smelly in summer and hard and cracked in winter. In 1839, the American inventor Charles Goodyear found that heating rubber with sulphur made it tough and stable. This process, called vulcanisation, made rubber useful for erasers, [[@tyres|tyres]], boots and much more.

In 1858, an American named Hymen Lipman patented a pencil with an eraser fitted into one end. In 1875, the US Supreme Court ruled that the patent was invalid, because joining two existing things wasn't a true invention. Pencils with erasers on top became common anyway, especially in American schools.

sec.h: What erasers are made of now
sec.t:
Most erasers today aren't natural rubber. Many are made of vinyl, a kind of [[@plastic-made|plastic]], mixed with softeners. Vinyl erasers are usually white, rub out cleanly and leave fewer smudges. Others use synthetic rubber made in factories from chemicals that come from oil. Fancy erasers shaped like fruit or animals are popular in schools, but they are often harder and smear more than plain ones.

Pink erasers often contain a little fine grit to help lift graphite. Kneaded erasers, used by artists, are soft and stretchy like dough. You press them onto a drawing to lighten areas without rubbing at all.

Pen ink is a liquid that soaks into the paper's fibres and dries there. A soft eraser can't reach it. Ink erasers contain rough grit that grinds away the top layer of paper along with the ink. They often leave a thin or fuzzy patch, and can tear the page.

Some school pens use special erasable ink that fades when it's warmed by [[@friction|friction]]. Rubbing creates heat, and the heat makes the ink turn clear. Put the paper in a freezer, and some of the "erased" writing can come back.

text: A cold starts when a virus lands in your nose or throat and gets inside the cells that line it. Your body notices and reacts quickly. Blood vessels in the lining of your nose widen and leak fluid. [[gland|Glands]] start making much more [[mucus|mucus]] than usual.

The result is a runny nose. All that liquid is a flood meant to trap the viruses and wash them out. Some goes down your throat, where stomach [[acid|acid]] destroys the viruses. The rest ends up in a tissue. The stuffy feeling comes from the swollen lining, not from mucus alone. Most of what makes you feel rotten in a cold is your own body fighting back.

st.reveal: The green colour comes from a substance inside white blood cells that pour into your nose to fight. It shows your immune system is busy. It doesn't mean you have a bacterial infection or need antibiotics.

d.try: Rub a little cooking oil and a pinch of glitter on your hands. Then wash them with water only for 20 seconds and see how much is left. Try again with soap. The glitter is like germs, and soap is much better at shifting them.
myth: Going out in the cold or with wet hair gives you a cold.

Colds are caused by viruses, so you can only catch one from a person who has the virus. Colds are more common in winter partly because people crowd together indoors, and cold air may make the nose's defences a little weaker.
facts: about 2 or 3 for adults, more for young children

sec.t:
Your nose makes mucus every day, even when you are well. It's sticky so it can catch dust, [[pollen|pollen]] and germs before they reach your lungs. Tiny hairs sweep it backwards, and you swallow it without noticing.

During a cold, the mucus gets thicker and changes colour. Yellow or [[@gross-snot|green snot]] comes from white blood cells that have rushed to fight. They contain an [[enzyme|enzyme]] with a greenish colour. So green snot means the battle is well under way, not that something worse has started. Your [[@sneezes|sneezes]] help too, blasting out mucus and viruses in a burst.

Flu, short for influenza, is caused by a different family of viruses. It often comes on suddenly, with a high [[@fever|fever]], aches all over and deep tiredness that can last a week or more. For most healthy children it passes, but it can be serious for babies, older people and people with other illnesses.

In 1918, near the end of the [[@world-war-one|First World War]], a flu [[pandemic|pandemic]] swept around the world. India was hit very hard, with millions of deaths. Flu viruses change their outer coats a little every year. That is why doctors recommend a new flu vaccine each year, especially for people most at risk.

There is no cure for a cold. Your body clears it, usually within a week to ten days. Rest, warm drinks and plenty of water can make you feel better. A spoon of honey in warm water can soothe a cough in children over one year old, though babies under one should never be given honey. [[@antibiotics|Antibiotics]] don't help, because they kill bacteria, and colds are caused by viruses. Taking them when they're not needed helps germs learn to resist them.

The best way to avoid colds is to stop the virus reaching your nose. Cold viruses spread through droplets when people cough and sneeze, and on hands and surfaces. Washing your hands with [[@soap-germs|soap]], coughing into your elbow and not rubbing your eyes and nose all make a difference.

text: छींक नाक से किसी अनचाही चीज़ को धमाके के साथ बाहर निकालने का शरीर का तरीका है। नाक की अंदरूनी परत [[nerve|नसों]] के सिरों से भरी होती है। जब धूल, [[pollen|पराग]], चुटकी भर काली मिर्च या ज़ुकाम का वायरस इन्हें छेड़ता है, तो ये ब्रेनस्टेम को संदेश भेजते हैं। ब्रेनस्टेम दिमाग़ का वह हिस्सा है जो अपने आप होने वाले काम चलाता है।

अब ब्रेनस्टेम कमान सँभाल लेता है। तुम एक गहरी साँस खींचते हो, छाती की [[@muscles|मांसपेशियाँ]] ज़ोर से भिंचती हैं, जीभ तालू से सट जाती है, और हवा धड़ाम से नाक के रास्ते बाहर निकल जाती है। आँखें भी झट से बंद हो जाती हैं। यह सब लगभग एक सेकंड में होता है। यह एक [[@reflexes|प्रतिवर्त क्रिया]] है, यानी तुम इसे करने का फ़ैसला नहीं करते।

sec.t:
अक्सर तुम्हें छींक आती हुई महसूस होती है। वह खुजली भरा, सनसनाता पल असल में नसों का संदेश है जो ज़ोर पकड़ रहा होता है। कुछ लोग उस समय नाक के नीचे दबाकर या [[@body-breath-hold|साँस रोककर]] छींक रोक लेते हैं। पर एक बार गहरी साँस अंदर खिंचने लगे, तो छींक लगभग हमेशा पूरी होकर ही रहती है।

नाक दबाकर और मुँह बंद करके पूरी छींक अंदर रोकना ठीक नहीं है। डॉक्टरों ने कुछ दुर्लभ मामले दर्ज किए हैं, जिनमें फँसे हुए दबाव से किसी के कानों या गले को चोट पहुँची। बेहतर है कि छींक को बाहर आने दो, रुमाल या टिश्यू में, या अपनी कोहनी में।

एक छींक में [[mucus|बलगम]] और [[saliva|लार]] की हज़ारों नन्ही बूँदें होती हैं। अमेरिका के मैसाचुसेट्स इंस्टिट्यूट ऑफ़ टेक्नोलॉजी के वैज्ञानिकों ने बहुत तेज़ रफ़्तार वाले [[@cameras-how|कैमरों]] से छींकों को फ़िल्माया है। उन्होंने पाया कि बूँदें गरम, नम हवा के एक गुबार के अंदर सफ़र करती हैं, जो सबसे छोटी बूँदों को कमरे में कई मीटर तक ले जा सकता है।

इसीलिए [[@cold-flu|ज़ुकाम]] और फ़्लू फैलने का एक बड़ा रास्ता छींक है। पुरानी किताबें दावा करती थीं कि छींक तेज़ दौड़ती कार से भी तेज़ निकलती है। असली रफ़्तार नापना मुश्किल है और यह बहुत बदलती रहती है, पर ज़्यादा चिंता की बात फैलता हुआ गुबार है। कोहनी में छींकने से इसका ज़्यादातर हिस्सा रुक जाता है। टिश्यू और भी बेहतर है, बशर्ते वह फ़ौरन कूड़ेदान में जाए और तुम हाथ धो लो।

कोविड-19 [[pandemic|महामारी]] के दौरान इन फ़िल्मों से यह समझने में मदद मिली कि मास्क और खुली खिड़कियाँ क्यों ज़रूरी हैं। बंद कमरे में छींक की बूँदें कुछ देर हवा में लटकी रहती हैं, जबकि चलती हवा उन्हें बहा ले जाती है।

sec.h: धूप वाली छींक और दूसरी अजीब बातें
sec.t:
हे फ़ीवर वाले लोगों को पराग से छींकें आती हैं। यह एक तरह की [[@allergies|एलर्जी]] है। काली मिर्च तो छींक की पुरानी उस्ताद है, क्योंकि उसके महीन कण नाक को छेड़ते हैं। इसी वजह से काली मिर्च, जो सारे [[@spices|मसालों]] में सबसे ज़्यादा बिकती रही है, सौ साल तक कार्टूनों के मज़ाक की पसंदीदा चीज़ बनी रही।

कुछ वजहें और भी अजीब हैं। तेज़ धूप से कुछ लोगों को छींक आती है, और कुछ लोग बहुत भारी खाना खाने के बाद छींकते हैं। कुछ लोग हमेशा लगातार दो-तीन बार छींकते हैं। 1981 में इंग्लैंड की डोना ग्रिफ़िथ्स नाम की एक लड़की ने छींकना शुरू किया और 978 दिन तक नहीं रुकी। आज भी इसे दर्ज किया गया सबसे लंबा छींकों का दौर माना जाता है।

बहुत-सी जगहों पर छींक के बाद लोग कोई भली बात कहते हैं। अंग्रेज़ी बोलने वाले "ब्लेस यू" कहते हैं, यानी भगवान तुम्हारा भला करे। जर्मन में "गेज़ुंडहाइट" कहते हैं, जिसका मतलब है सेहत, और स्पेनिश में "सालुद", जिसका मतलब भी यही है। ये रिवाज कहाँ से शुरू हुए, इस बारे में लोग अलग-अलग किस्से सुनाते हैं, और पक्का कोई नहीं जानता।

जानवर भी छींकते हैं। बिल्लियाँ और कुत्ते हमारी तरह ही नाक साफ़ करने के लिए छींकते हैं। अफ़्रीकी जंगली कुत्ते इससे भी आगे हैं। बोत्सवाना में हुए एक अध्ययन में पाया गया कि जब झुंड तय कर रहा होता था कि शिकार पर निकलें या नहीं, तो छींकें जितनी ज़्यादा होतीं, निकलने की संभावना उतनी बढ़ जाती। मानो वे छींककर वोट डाल रहे हों।

text: Superglue was found by a chemist named Harry Coover, not once but twice. In 1942, during the Second World War, his team at the Eastman Kodak company in the USA was trying to make clear plastic for the sights on guns. One substance, called cyanoacrylate, stuck to everything it touched, including the equipment. It was useless for gun sights, so they set it aside.

Nine years later, in 1951, Coover and a colleague, Fred Joyner, met the same chemical while hunting for a tough coating for jet aircraft. This time Coover saw what it really was: an extraordinarily strong [[@glue-sticky|glue]]. It went on sale in 1958.

st.reveal: Superglue hardens when it meets water, even the faint film of moisture found on skin and on most surfaces. That's why it grabs fingers so quickly and why the cap must be closed tight.

Pulling can tear the skin. The safe way is to soak the fingers in warm soapy water and gently roll them apart over a few minutes. Ask an adult to help, and get medical help if glue goes near the eyes or mouth.

sec.t:
The 1951 accident was an expensive one. Joyner spread a thin film of cyanoacrylate between two glass [[prism|prisms]] of a refractometer, an instrument that measures how light bends. He couldn't separate them again. The costly instrument was wrecked, and the team began testing the liquid on anything they could find.

Everything stuck. Metal to metal, glass to glass, rubber to wood, all in seconds and without heat or clamps. In 1958 Eastman sold it as "Eastman 910". A year later, on an American TV show called *I've Got a Secret*, Coover stuck two metal bars together with a single drop. Then he hung the show's host from them, lifting him off the ground.

Doctors soon noticed that a glue which sets on wet skin might close wounds. Early versions could irritate the body, but army medics in the Vietnam War used spray versions to slow bleeding on the battlefield. In 1998 the USA approved a special medical skin glue, and today doctors use similar glues to close some small cuts without stitches.

Coral scientists even use thick superglue gels underwater, to fix broken pieces of living coral back onto reefs.

Superglue's speed makes it tricky. Because it sets in seconds, there's little time to line pieces up, and a drop in the wrong place can glue your fingers to the thing you're fixing. It works best on small, tight joints, not on big gaps or on soft things like cloth.

It also gives off sharp fumes that can sting the eyes and nose, so it's best used with a window open, and with an adult. Nail polish remover can soften dried superglue, but an adult should use it and keep it well away from eyes.

Chemists have since made many kinds: gels that don't drip, slower versions that give you a few extra seconds, and bendy ones that don't crack when the object flexes.

In the late 1970s, police scientists noticed that superglue fumes in a closed space left white crusts on [[@fingerprints|fingerprints]]. The fumes react with the tiny traces of water and oil a finger leaves behind, building a white plastic copy of every ridge. Detectives now place objects in a box, warm a few drops of glue, and wait for invisible prints to appear.

Coover was honoured with America's National Medal of Technology and Innovation in 2010. And the strangest part? About ten years after superglue went on sale, another chemist made a glue so weak it was almost a failure, and it became the [[@accident-post-it|sticky note]].

text: A hackathon is an event where people team up to build something new with technology in a short time, usually 24 to 48 hours. The name joins "hack", which programmers use to mean a clever, quick piece of work, with "marathon".

Teams pick a problem, sketch an idea, write code and show a working demo at the end. Judges choose winners, but many people go just to learn, make friends and see what they can build when the clock is ticking.

st.prompt: In the word "hackathon", what does "hack" mean?

options.t: Chopping up old code with a delete key

st.reveal: Among programmers, a hack has long meant a quick, clever fix or project. The criminal meaning came later. A hackathon is a marathon of the good kind of hacking.

d.try: Run a mini "paper hackathon" with friends. Pick a small problem, such as forgetting your water bottle, and give yourselves 30 minutes to design an app or gadget that solves it. Draw the screens on paper and present your idea in one minute.
myth: Hackathons are contests for people who break into computer systems.
Hackathons are about making things, such as apps, websites or gadgets. Some security events do test systems, but only with permission and under strict rules.

sec.t:
Most hackathons start with a theme. It might be healthier cities, cleaner rivers or helping older people use phones. Teams of two to five people then brainstorm, split the work and start building.

One person might design the screens. Another writes the code that makes buttons work. Someone else prepares the presentation. Organisers provide desks, Wi-Fi, power sockets, food and mentors who help when teams get stuck. At the end, each team gets a few minutes to show judges what they made.

India runs one of the world's biggest. The Smart India Hackathon, organised by the central government since 2017, asks college students to solve problems set by ministries and companies, such as tracking water use or making railway services smoother. Hundreds of thousands of students have taken part over the years.

NASA runs the Space Apps Challenge every year, with events in cities on every inhabited continent. In its first year, 2012, it even had a location in Antarctica. Teams use real NASA data to build tools, such as maps of wildfires or apps that show where the International Space Station is. Students in Bengaluru, Pune, Texas and Kenya might be working on the same challenge on the same weekend.

You don't need to be an expert programmer to join. Teams need people who can draw, explain ideas, test apps and think about who will use them. Some hackathons are for school students and use friendly block-coding tools like [[@python-scratch|Scratch]], where you snap commands together like puzzle pieces. A ten-year-old can build a simple game in an afternoon that way, and many school hackathons give prizes for the best idea, not the fanciest code.

Others focus on hardware, where teams build gadgets with small computer boards, [[sensor|sensors]] and motors. Some are about art, music or games. Many teams reuse free code from [[@open-source|open-source]] projects, so they don't have to start every piece from scratch.

Most hackathon projects are rough demos that never go further. That's fine, because the point is to try ideas fast and learn. But some do grow into real products, and a few teams have gone on to start companies, which is how many [[@startups-entrepreneurs|startups]] begin.

Long events can mean staying up all night. Good organisers now set up quiet rooms and remind people to rest, because tired brains make more mistakes. Scientists who study [[@sleep-why|sleep]] say it's when your brain sorts and stores what it learned that day, which matters even when you're racing a deadline. Making an [[@apps-made|app]] is easier with a clear head.

text: On 13 April 1919, thousands of people gathered in Jallianwala Bagh, a walled open ground in Amritsar, near the Golden Temple. Some had come for a peaceful protest meeting. Many were families visiting the city for Baisakhi, a spring harvest festival and a special day for Sikhs.

Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer arrived with soldiers, blocked the main entrance and, without warning, ordered them to fire. They fired for about ten minutes, until their ammunition was nearly used up. The official count was 379 dead, but Indian inquiries believed about 1,000 died, with many more wounded. The massacre turned millions of Indians against British rule.

st.prompt: How did many people in Britain react to General Dyer after the massacre?

options.t: Some condemned him, but others praised him and raised money for him
Everyone agreed he should be put in prison
Nobody in Britain heard about it for 50 years

st.reveal: The Hunter Committee criticised Dyer and he was forced to leave the army. But some politicians defended him, and a British newspaper raised a large sum of money as a gift for him. The split shocked many Indians.

src.Kim A. Wagner, Amritsar 1919: An Empire of Fear and the Making of a Massacre (Yale University Press, 2019).

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.
n.certNote: The main events are not in doubt. The number of people killed is disputed. The official British inquiry counted 379 dead, while the Indian National Congress's own inquiry estimated about 1,000.

myth: The people in Jallianwala Bagh had gathered for a riot.
Most of the crowd were unarmed. Many had come for a peaceful protest meeting, and many others were visitors in Amritsar for the Baisakhi festival, unaware of a ban on gatherings.

sec.t:
During the [[@world-war-one|First World War]], more than a million Indians served in the British army. Many Indians hoped for more self-rule afterwards. Instead, in March 1919, the government passed the Rowlatt Act, which let officials jail people suspected of political activity without trial.

Mahatma [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] called for peaceful protests across India. In Amritsar, two popular local leaders, Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr Satyapal, were arrested on 10 April. Crowds protested, some turned violent, and several people, both Indian and British, were killed. The British imposed strict control and banned public meetings, but the ban was poorly announced, and many people did not know about it.

At first, news spread slowly, because [[@punjab|Punjab]] was under martial law. When it came out, there was outrage. The poet [[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]] wrote to the Viceroy, giving up the knighthood he had received in 1915. He said he wanted to stand beside his countrymen.

The British government set up the Hunter Committee to investigate. Dyer told it that he had wanted to make a strong impression on the whole of Punjab. The committee criticised him, and he was removed from his command. Yet many in Britain treated him as a hero, and a newspaper collected money for him.

The massacre changed the [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]]. Many Indians who had trusted British promises now wanted full independence. In 1920 Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation Movement, asking Indians to boycott British courts, schools and goods.

A well-known story says that a 12-year-old boy named [[@bhagat-singh|Bhagat Singh]] visited the garden soon after and took home a little of its soil. Years later, in 1940, a man named Udham Singh shot dead Michael O'Dwyer, who had governed Punjab in 1919, in London.

Jallianwala Bagh is now a national memorial with a tall flame-shaped monument, opened in 1961. Visitors can see the narrow entrance, the walls with bullet marks and the Martyrs' Well.

British leaders have since called the massacre shameful. In 2019, its 100th anniversary, Prime Minister Theresa May called it a "shameful scar" on British Indian history, though the British government has not made a formal apology. Every 13 April, people gather in the garden to remember.

text: Nobody knows the full answer yet. What scientists do know is that the bones at Roopkund came from several groups of people who died in different centuries.

A study in 2019 tested the DNA of 38 skeletons. Most belonged to people with South Asian ancestry who died between about 800 and 1000 CE. A second group, who died roughly 200 years ago, had ancestry like people from Greece and Crete today. One person had East Asian or Southeast Asian ancestry. How each group died, and why the Mediterranean group was there at all, is still a puzzle.

st.prompt: When scientists tested the DNA of the Roopkund skeletons in 2019, what did they find?

options.t: Different groups who died about a thousand years apart
One army that died all on the same day

st.reveal: Many people had assumed everyone died in one disaster. The DNA and carbon dating showed at least three groups. One died roughly 1,200 years ago, while another died only around 200 years ago.

src: Harney É. et al. (2019) Ancient DNA from the skeletons of Roopkund Lake reveals Mediterranean migrants in India. Nature Communications.

n.certNote: Scientists agree the bones belong to several groups who died at different times, about a thousand years apart. Exactly how each group died is still unknown. A deadly hailstorm is one popular idea for some of the deaths, but it has not been proven.

sec.t:
Roopkund sits at about 5,000 m in the Himalaya of Uttarakhand, below the peak of Trishul. It is small, about 40 m across, and frozen for much of the year. When the snow melts each summer, bones show through the ice and the rocky slopes around it.

In 1942, a forest ranger named H. K. Madhwal came across the lake and was shocked. Hundreds of skeletons lay in and around the water. Some still had hair, bits of skin and even shoes, preserved by the cold. Because it was the Second World War, some people first guessed they were Japanese soldiers who had sneaked into India. They weren't.

Then came the 2019 study, by scientists from India, the USA and Europe. They pulled ancient [[@dna|DNA]] from the bones and used [[@half-life|carbon dating]] to work out when each person died.

The results surprised everyone. The deaths were not all at once. The South Asian group seemed to have died in several events over a long period. The Mediterranean group died around 1800 CE. Chemicals locked in the bones showed that the groups had also eaten quite different diets during their lives. They were not one party of travellers.

Roopkund lies on the route of the Nanda Devi Raj Jat, a [[pilgrimage|pilgrimage]] held roughly every 12 years. Thousands of people walk for about three weeks into the high mountains to honour the goddess Nanda Devi.

Many scientists think at least some of the South Asian group may have been pilgrims on an early form of this journey. But nobody has found records of the route that far back. And it is still unclear why people with Mediterranean ancestry were walking in the high Himalaya around 1800 CE.

Over the years, trekkers took bones and other remains as souvenirs, and some remains have been disturbed. Today the area is better protected, and visitors are asked to leave everything where it is.

Roopkund is a hard trek, and the thin air at that height can make people ill. Walkers usually climb slowly over several days to let their bodies adjust. Whoever died there had climbed into one of the harshest places in India. Each breath at that height holds only about half the oxygen of a breath on a Mumbai street, as the science of [[@altitude|altitude]] explains.

text: Ethiopia is a big country in the Horn of Africa, the part of East Africa that sticks out towards Arabia. Much of it is a high plateau, with mountains and deep gorges, and the capital, Addis Ababa, sits about 2,350 metres above the sea. With around 13 crore people, it has the second-largest population in Africa.

Ethiopia is unusual in many ways. It was never turned into a European colony, apart from a short Italian occupation from 1936 to 1941. It has its own ancient script, its own calendar and its own way of telling the time. It is the homeland of arabica coffee, and some of the oldest [[fossil|fossils]] of human ancestors have been found in its dry north-east.

st.prompt: In Ethiopian time, the day starts counting at sunrise. If a friend in Addis Ababa says "let's meet at 2 o'clock in the morning", when should you go?
st.reveal: In the traditional Ethiopian clock, the first hour of the day starts at about 6 a.m., when the sun rises near the equator. So 2 o'clock in Ethiopian time is about 8 a.m. on most clocks. Many people in cities switch between both systems.

sec.t:
The Ethiopian calendar has 12 months of 30 days each, plus a short 13th month of five days, or six in a leap year. Tourist posters once used the slogan "13 months of sunshine". New Year falls in September, after the long rains end. The calendar counts years about seven to eight years behind the Gregorian one used in India and the USA, because it dates the birth of Jesus differently.

The clock is different too. Near the [[equator|equator]], days and nights are almost the same length all year, so traditional Ethiopian time starts counting the hours at sunrise. One o'clock in the morning means one hour after dawn. Few [[@calendars|calendars]] on Earth work quite like it.

In 1974, scientists in the Afar region found much of the skeleton of a human ancestor who lived about 3.2 million years ago. They nicknamed her Lucy, after a [[@beatles-music|Beatles]] song playing at their camp. Ethiopians call her Dinkinesh, meaning "you are marvellous". She walked upright, and she helped show that our ancestors walked on two legs long before their brains grew large, an important clue in [[@human-evolution|human evolution]].

Wild arabica [[@coffee|coffee]] still grows in Ethiopia's south-western forests. In a traditional coffee ceremony, the host roasts green beans over a small fire, grinds them by hand and brews them three times in a clay pot, while incense burns nearby.

The national food is injera, a big, spongy, slightly sour flatbread made from teff, a grain even smaller than most [[@millets|millets]]. Stews are spooned on top, and everyone tears off pieces of injera to scoop them up.

Ethiopian writing uses the Ge'ez script, an [[abugida|abugida]], in which each symbol stands for a consonant plus a vowel, a bit like Devanagari. And Ethiopia is famous for runners. In 1960, Abebe Bikila won the Olympic [[@running-marathon|marathon]] in Rome running barefoot, and Ethiopian athletes have won long-distance races ever since.

text: Pangong Tso is a long, narrow lake high in the Himalayas, shared between [[@ladakh|Ladakh]] in India and Tibet in China. It sits about 4,250 metres above sea level, higher than many of the clouds you see from a city.

It seems to change colour because light keeps changing. Clear, deep water soaks up red and yellow light and sends back blue. Shallow water over pale mud looks turquoise or green. When a cloud passes, the lake turns grey. At that height the sunlight is very strong and the air is very clear, so every change looks sharper than it would at a lake in the plains.

Green fish swimming near the surface

st.reveal: Deep, clear water soaks up red light and looks rich blue. In shallow parts, light bounces off the pale lake bed and fine mud, so the water looks turquoise or green. Clouds and the angle of the sun change it again through the day.

The water itself stays much the same. What changes is the light, meaning the sun's angle, clouds overhead, wind ripples and how deep you are looking. Your eyes see a different mix of reflected and scattered colours as these change.

sec.h: A salty lake in the sky
sec.t:
Pangong is about 134 kilometres long, a little shorter than the road from Mumbai to Nashik. Yet in many places it is only a few kilometres wide. Its water is brackish, a little salty, because streams flow in but no river flows out. Water leaves only by [[evaporation|evaporation]], and the salt is left behind.

Very few fish live in the salty water on the Indian side. The lake still draws life, though. In summer, [[@bar-headed-goose|bar-headed geese]], Brahminy ducks and gulls nest on its shores. Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas twice a year, at heights where a person would struggle to breathe.

Salt usually stops water from freezing easily. But Ladakh's winter nights fall well below −20 °C, cold enough to freeze Pangong's surface solid from about January to March. The ice can be thick enough to walk on.

In February 2023, runners took part in a 21-kilometre race across the frozen lake. It was called the Last Run and was billed as the world's highest frozen-lake half-marathon. The organisers wanted to draw attention to how [[climate|climate]] change is affecting the Himalayas.

To reach Pangong from Leh, visitors cross the Chang La pass, more than 5,300 metres high. At that [[@altitude|altitude]], each breath carries only about half the oxygen it would at sea level. Many travellers get headaches, and guides tell them to rest in Leh for a day or two before going higher.

The lake became famous across India after the 2009 Hindi film 3 Idiots filmed its last scene on the shore. Tourist numbers shot up. Today, camps, cafés and a road busy with jeeps line the shore in summer.

Pangong lies in a valley left by the slow crash of India into Asia, which pushed up the Himalayas. Long ago, scientists think, the lake drained into a river. Then the land shifted, the outlet was blocked, and the water had nowhere to go.

The border between India and China runs across the lake, and the two countries disagree about exactly where it lies, so parts are closed to visitors. And the strangest part? Not far away, people walk for days along a frozen river gorge on the [[@india-wonder-chadar-trek|Chadar trek]].

text: Most messages today are texts, emails and voice notes. Yet people still write letters by hand. A letter is slow and takes effort, and that is exactly why it feels special. You can hold it, keep it in a drawer and read it again years later.

People also write letters for practical reasons. Courts, banks and governments still send official letters. Many children write to Santa or to their favourite authors. And for soldiers, prisoners and people in remote places, a letter can still be the best way to hear from home.

sec.t:
In the summer of 1928, Jawaharlal [[@nehru|Nehru]] was in Allahabad while his daughter Indira was at school in Mussoorie. He wrote her long letters about how the Earth was formed, how early humans lived and how languages grew.

The next year they were printed as *Letters from a Father to His Daughter*. Indira grew up to become India's prime minister, and the book is still read by children. Nehru wrote to her from prison too, and those letters became a much longer history of the world.

An [[@email|email]] arrives in seconds. A letter takes days. Some people think that wait is part of the charm. Writing slowly also changes what you say. You choose your words more carefully when you can't press delete.

Some scientists have studied whether writing by hand helps you remember better than typing. Several studies suggest it does, perhaps because handwriting makes you slow down and think about each idea. Researchers are still arguing about how big the effect is.

Many famous letters are now treasured in museums. Abraham Lincoln wrote letters that people still quote. In 1939 Albert Einstein signed a letter warning the US president about atomic weapons. Anne Frank, hiding from the Nazis, wrote her diary partly as letters to an imaginary friend called Kitty.

Historians love letters because they show what ordinary people thought at the time, in their own handwriting and [[@ink|ink]]. A soldier's note home or a farmer's letter to a son in the city can tell us more than an official report.

A pen pal is a friend you get to know by writing. Some schools in India and the United States link classes so pupils can swap letters across oceans. Many people collect stamps or postcards from the places they visit. Stamp collecting, called philately, can teach you a surprising amount of history and geography.

Writing a letter needs little: paper, a pen, an envelope and a stamp. An inland letter card in India still costs only a few rupees to send anywhere in the country. For that price, someone far away gets a piece of paper that you once held in your hands.

text: A newspaper is made in a rush every day. [[@journalism|Reporters]] find and check stories. Editors decide which ones matter most and fix the writing. Designers fit the stories, photos and adverts onto pages. Late at night, the pages are sent to a printing plant.

Giant presses print on rolls of paper, folding and cutting the pages as they go. Before dawn, vans carry bundles to distributors and newsstands. By breakfast, a delivery person has dropped the paper at your door.

Good newspapers check facts carefully and print corrections when they get things wrong, but mistakes still happen. Some papers also take sides. Reading more than one source is the best way to get close to the truth.

sec.t:
The day often starts with a meeting where editors plan the next morning's paper. Reporters go out to courts, police stations, government offices, stadiums and neighbourhoods. They interview people, read documents and take notes.

A good reporter checks each important fact, ideally with more than one source. Back in the office, sub-editors (copy editors in the US) tighten the writing, check names and numbers, and write headlines. A headline has to tell a story in a few words and fit into a fixed space.

As the deadline gets close, things move fast. If big news breaks late, a page may be redone at the last minute. The front page is usually the last to be finished.

Once the pages are designed, each one is turned into a thin metal plate. Newspaper presses are huge machines, often several storeys tall. They use rolls of paper, called reels, that can weigh around a tonne each and unroll for kilometres.

The paper races through rollers that print both sides at once, in four ink colours: cyan, magenta, yellow and black. Further down the line, machines cut, fold and stack the papers. A big press can print tens of thousands of copies in an hour.

Newspaper paper, called newsprint, is thin and cheap, made from wood pulp or recycled paper. That keeps the price low enough to be thrown away tomorrow.

{{story:fake-news}}

In [[@ancient-rome|ancient Rome]], from 59 BCE, the government posted handwritten notices called the Acta Diurna, "daily acts", in public places. China's imperial court sent out bulletins to officials for many centuries.

After the [[@printing-press|printing press]] came to Europe, printed news sheets followed. The World Association of News Publishers recognises Relation, printed in Strasbourg from 1605, as the first newspaper. In America, the Boston News-Letter began in 1704.

[[@hist-first-newspaper-india|India's first newspaper]], Hicky's Bengal Gazette, was started in Calcutta in 1780 by an Irishman, James Augustus Hicky. It was full of gossip and attacks on the officials of the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]], especially the Governor-General, Warren Hastings. In 1782 Hicky's printing press was seized and the paper closed.

Dozens of papers in Indian languages followed in the 1800s. During the [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]], newspapers became powerful. Bal Gangadhar Tilak published Kesari in Marathi, and Mahatma [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] edited Young India and Harijan. The British sometimes shut papers down or jailed editors for what they printed.

Today, most people read news on phones and websites, which are updated all day. Many papers sell fewer printed copies than they used to. In India, though, printed newspapers have stayed strong compared with many countries, and papers appear in dozens of languages.

The basic job hasn't changed. Find out what happened, check it, explain it clearly and make it [[@news-media|news]] people can trust. A printed page can't be quietly edited later, which is one reason some readers still prefer it.

text: The oldest noodles ever found come from China. In 2005, scientists reported a bowl of thin, yellow noodles at Lajia, a site on the Yellow River in northwest China. An earthquake and flood about 4,000 years ago had buried the village. The bowl was upside down in the mud, and the noodles had stayed sealed underneath.

Tests suggested they were made from millet, a small grain that grew well in northern China. Later, Chinese cooks made noodles mostly from wheat. In Italy and the Arab world, people made their own kinds of pasta, probably without any help from China.

sec.t:
Noodles became central to Chinese food over thousands of years. By about 2,000 years ago, people in China were making wheat noodles. In northern China, cooks still stretch and fold dough by hand into hundreds of thin strands, called lamian.

In China and other parts of East Asia, long noodles are a symbol of long life. People eat them on [[@life-birthdays-world|birthdays]] and try not to cut them. Noodles spread to Japan, Korea and Southeast Asia, each place making its own kind, from Japanese [[@maggi-noodles|ramen]] to [[@vietnam|Vietnamese]] pho.

Italian pasta has its own story. A geographer named al-Idrisi, writing in 1154 for the king of Sicily, described a town near Palermo where people made dried pasta and shipped it around the Mediterranean. Sicily had been ruled by Arabs for about 200 years, and they knew how to dry noodles for long journeys.

Dried pasta is made from durum wheat, a very hard wheat that holds its shape when cooked. Italy now has hundreds of shapes, from spaghetti, meaning "little strings", to bow-shaped farfalle, meaning "butterflies".

Many people believe [[@marco-polo|Marco Polo]] brought pasta back from China. But he returned in 1295, and pasta was already being made in Italy long before. Historians traced the story to an article in an American pasta trade magazine in 1929.

{{story:marco-polo}}

In 1958, Momofuku Ando, a businessman in Osaka, Japan, invented instant noodles after a year of experiments in a shed behind his house. He found that frying cooked noodles dried them out and left tiny holes. Hot water could then soften them in minutes.

In 1971, he launched Cup Noodles, sold in a cup with a lid. Instant noodles are now eaten around the world, with more than 100 billion servings eaten each year (2020s figures). In 2005, a version was made for the Japanese astronaut Soichi Noguchi to eat on the Space Shuttle, as you can read in [[@space-food|space food]].

India has noodles of its own. Seviyan, thin wheat strands, are cooked with milk and sugar as a sweet, especially at Eid. In [[@kerala|Kerala]] and Tamil Nadu, idiyappam, made by pressing rice dough into fine strings and steaming it, is a breakfast dish. Crispy sev, made from gram flour, is a snack.

Chinese immigrants who settled in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] more than two centuries ago helped create Indo-Chinese food, including hakka noodles and chilli chicken. Instant noodles arrived in India in the 1980s and quickly became an after-school favourite.

The first noodles were made from [[@millets|millet]], and millets are becoming popular again. They grow with little water and are packed with fibre and minerals. Some Indian companies now make noodles from ragi, jowar and other millets, which would not have looked strange to cooks at Lajia 4,000 years ago.
